newsitem.title: INDIA: Afghan opposition advancing north of Kabul - envoy.
newsitem.headline: Afghan opposition advancing north of Kabul - envoy.

text.p: Opposition forces control Afghanistan's northern provinces and are advancing against the Taleban militia north of the capital Kabul, ousted President Burhanuddin Rabbani's ambassador to India said on Friday.

Masood Khalili told a news conference that opposition forces were advancing towards the Soviet-built airbase of Bagram and Charikar, about 50 km (30 miles) north of Kabul, after consolidating their hold over the northern provinces.
"Today we are four kilometres from Bagram," the diplomat said. "We are now fighting north of Kabul, not in northern Afghanistan."
Asked when opposition forces might reach Kabul, Khalili said: "It is too early to say. We are very cautious. It is still a very bad time for moving."
The envoy said opposition forces loyal to Tajik guerrilla commander Ahmad Shah Masood were firmly in control of the strategic Salang Pass, about 100 km (60 miles) north of Kabul.

He said they took Pul-i-Khumri town, north of the pass, overnight and Taleban Islamic forces were trapped between Pul-i-Khumri and the Salang Pass. "It is impossible for them to get out as Salang is blocked," he said.
Earlier on Friday, a Pakistan-based Afghan news service said Masood's forces had captured the strategic town of Jabal-os-Siraj, north of Charikar, from Taleban militia.
The Afghan Islamic Press (AIP) quoted sources in Afghanistan as saying opposition forces had also seized Golbahar, at the mouth of Masood's native Panjsher Valley.
Khalili said 388 Taleban fighters were either captured or killed in Golbahar.
He said Rabbani, who earlier this week was reported to be in neighbouring Tajikistan, was now in northern Afghanistan.

The diplomat said opposition forces had killed or captured 5,000 Taleban fighters, including some Pakistani nationals, in clashes in recent days, and captured Taleban Information Minister Amir Khan Mutaqi in fighting near Pul-i-Khumri.
Khalili said opposition forces had engaged the Taleban on a second front in northwestern Afghanistan near Qala-i-Nau, capital of Badghis province.

Shops in Herat city, also in the northwest and controlled by the Taleban, were closed on Thursday. "Some movement of people, though they are disarmed, has started. It reminds me of another rebellion of the people," he said.
Khalili said the opposition's rapid advances since they recaptured the northern city of Mazar-i-Sharif on Wednesday had dramatically changed the strategic situation.
"We are back to where we were eight months ago but with one difference -- 5,000 enemy forces have been captured or killed," he said.
"I think we are now stronger than before, more united. I think the tide is very much against them. I don't think their people can stop it."
He said the presence of Pakistanis among Taleban militia who took over Mazar-i-Sharif last weekend had spurred opposition to the militia in the northern city.

Uzbek General Abdul Malik had defected from the opposition, helping the purist Islamic militia take hold of Mazar-i-Sharif, but he later turned on the Taleban and chased them out of the city on Wednesday.
Khalili said Malik and Masood were now coordinating their efforts to defeat Taleban. "We trust him," the envoy said of Malik.
